– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The test `testEqualsCS1()` contains assertions that check equality for CharSequence instances, including StringBuilder objects of various lengths. Notably, it asserts `false` for two CharSequences of different lengths (e.g., "abc" vs "abcd"). The method under test is `StringUtils.equals(CharSequence cs1, CharSequence cs2)`. Inspection of this method reveals that if both are not String instances, it delegates to `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches()` using the maximum length of the two CharSequences as the length to compare.

Looking at `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches()`, the method attempts to match regions of the provided CharSequences character by character up to the given length. However, it does not check whether the 'length' parameter exceeds either CharSequence's length before calling `charAt` on them. This results in an attempt to access indices beyond the valid length of one of the CharSequences when their lengths differ and the maximum length is used, causing a StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Therefore, the bug occurs because `StringUtils.equals` uses the maximum length of the two CharSequences for region comparison, but `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches` assumes the passed length is valid for both sequences. This causes `charAt` to throw an exception when sequences of different lengths are compared.

The failing test `Assert.assertFalse(StringUtils.equals(new StringBuilder("abc"), new StringBuilder("abcd")));` triggers the bug because it compares sequences of different lengths, and the current implementation incorrectly passes length 4 (max length) to `regionMatches`, which tries to access index 3 on the shorter sequence of length 3.

This root cause matches the current bug report's description about String Index OBE when sequences differ in length. Recent bug reports do not seem relevant to this exact problem.

The fix should ensure that `StringUtils.equals` uses the minimum length for the region comparison or modify `regionMatches` to safely handle differing lengths. However, according to string equality semantics, sequences with different lengths should immediately return false, so a length check comparing the lengths would be better.

In summary, the bug is from misuse of length parameter in `StringUtils.equals` when delegating to `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches`, causing invalid index access on shorter CharSequence.

Next, I will suggest which methods should be fixed.
org.apache.commons.codec.binary.StringUtils.equals(java.lang.CharSequence,java.lang.CharSequence)
org.apache.commons.codec.binary.CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches(java.lang.CharSequence,boolean,int,java.lang.CharSequence,int,int)

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
